title: Yusuf's Astonishing Sentence to the Brothers Who Sold Him
script: Narrator: [measured] Decades separate the well into which Yusuf was lowered from the palace hall in which his brothers, unrecognizing, eventually stood before him, and that distance is precisely the point.
Narrator: [reflective] He had every instrument of retribution available by then: the authority of Egypt, their evident poverty, and the irony of their ignorance of who governed the grain they needed.

Narrator: [thoughtful] Instead, he orchestrated a slow, theatrical unveiling, testing them not out of cruelty but, one suspects, to discover whether the men who had betrayed him still existed inside these older faces.

Narrator: [firm] When he finally disclosed himself, the sentence he offered wasn't absolution dressed as magnanimity; it was strikingly specific: no blame will be upon you today, a phrase that names the wrong rather than dissolving it into vague forgiveness.

Narrator: [reflective] That specificity matters enormously. He doesn't pretend the well never happened, or that grief hadn't aged his father blind with weeping; he simply declines to let that history dictate what happens next.

Narrator: [thoughtful] Consider, too, what preceded this moment: years of imprisonment on a false accusation, years he could easily have narrated as proof that decency accomplishes nothing in an indifferent world.
Narrator: [warm] He might reasonably have concluded that integrity is a poor investment, given how consistently it earned him wells, prisons, and slander rather than reward.

Narrator: [reflective] Instead, each trial seems to have refined rather than embittered him, so that by the time forgiveness becomes possible, it emerges not as reluctant concession but as settled character.

Narrator: [thoughtful] There's also his father, Ya'qub, whose grief across those decades was never portrayed as excessive or embarrassing, weeping until his eyes clouded, holding out hope long after hope seemed reasonable.
Narrator: [warm] The reunion, when it arrives, restores not merely a lost son but a father's stubborn, unfashionable insistence that patience beautifully borne is never ultimately wasted.

Narrator: [reflective] What lingers with me isn't the forgiveness alone but its architecture: specific naming of harm, followed by a deliberate, undramatic refusal to let that harm write the remaining chapters.
Narrator: [peacefully] Betrayal, this story insists, doesn't have to be the final authority on how a relationship, or a person, eventually turns out.

quiz.question: What material advantages did Yusuf have over his brothers when they finally stood before him?
options: None at all
The authority of Egypt, their poverty, and their ignorance of who governed the grain
Only his physical strength
A written confession from them
quiz.explanation: He had the authority of Egypt, their evident poverty, and the irony of their ignorance of who controlled the grain they needed.

quiz.question: What was the exact nature of Yusuf's declaration to his brothers?
options: A vague statement that nothing had ever happened
A specific phrase naming the wrong while declining to let it dictate the future
A demand for repayment first
A refusal to forgive them at all
quiz.explanation: His phrase, 'no blame will be upon you today,' names the wrong specifically rather than dissolving it into vague forgiveness.

quiz.question: What had Yusuf endured before this moment of reunion?
options: A comfortable life free of hardship
Years of imprisonment on a false accusation, in addition to being sold and enslaved
Only a brief period of difficulty
Exile from Egypt entirely
quiz.explanation: He had endured years of imprisonment on a false accusation, on top of being sold into slavery by his brothers.

quiz.question: How does the narrator describe the effect of Yusuf's trials on his character?
options: They embittered him permanently
Each trial seems to have refined rather than embittered him
They had no noticeable effect
They made him seek revenge eventually
quiz.explanation: The narrator says each trial seems to have refined rather than embittered him, so forgiveness emerged as settled character.

quiz.question: What does the narrator identify as the 'architecture' of Yusuf's forgiveness?
options: Pretending nothing happened, followed by silence
Specific naming of harm, followed by a deliberate refusal to let that harm write the remaining chapters
Public punishment followed by private forgiveness
Demanding an apology before forgiving
quiz.explanation: The narrator describes it as specific naming of harm, followed by a deliberate, undramatic refusal to let that harm dictate what comes next.

title: What Musa Learned From a Teacher Who Wouldn't Explain Himself
script: Amira: [curious] The story of Musa and Khidr unsettles me every time, Fajar, precisely because Musa is meant to be the more accomplished prophet of the two.

Fajar: [thoughtful] Which makes the premise deliberately uncomfortable. He's told there's knowledge he lacks, held by someone whose actions he'll be forbidden to question, on pain of the arrangement ending.
Amira: [pointed] And he agrees anyway, which strikes me as its own quiet act of humility, admitting a gap in understanding despite considerable stature.
Fajar: [nodding] Then, almost immediately, he fails the condition. Khidr damages a boat belonging to poor fishermen, and Musa, appalled, objects before he can stop himself.
Amira: [reflective] It's such a human failure, though. Watching an apparently senseless act of destruction and staying silent requires a discipline most of us simply don't possess.
Fajar: [considering] Khidr forgives the lapse once, reminding him of the agreement, and they continue, only for Musa to object again when Khidr kills a young boy without warning.
Amira: [somber] That one is genuinely difficult to sit with. The apparent cruelty of it resists easy explanation in the moment.
Fajar: [reflective] Which is exactly the point. Musa is reacting to what's visible, the immediate, undeniable wrongness of it, while Khidr operates from knowledge Musa simply doesn't possess yet.
Amira: [curious] And the explanations, once they arrive, do they actually satisfy you, or just relocate the discomfort somewhere else?
Fajar: [honestly] Somewhat both. The boat was damaged to protect it from a king seizing usable vessels; the boy would have grieved his righteous parents through cruelty and disbelief.
Amira: [thoughtful] So mercy, in both cases, was disguised as harm, legible only from a vantage point neither of them could occupy simultaneously.
Fajar: [warm] Exactly, and I think that's the real instruction here, not a lesson about specific miracles, but about the limits of judging events solely by their visible surface.

Amira: [reflective] It's humbling rather than comforting, honestly. It doesn't promise every senseless-looking hardship has a tidy explanation; it just insists our vantage point is narrower than we assume.
Fajar: [gently] Which is perhaps why Musa, of all people, needed this particular lesson. Confidence in one's own perception is exactly what such an episode is designed to unsettle.

quiz.question: What condition does Musa agree to before traveling with Khidr?
options: To pay for the journey himself
To not question Khidr's actions, on pain of the arrangement ending
To remain silent the entire journey
To bring provisions for both of them
quiz.explanation: Musa agrees not to question Khidr's actions, with the arrangement ending if he does.

quiz.question: What is the first action of Khidr's that Musa objects to?
options: Killing a young boy
Damaging a boat belonging to poor fishermen
Building a wall for no payment
Refusing to share food
quiz.explanation: Khidr damages a boat belonging to poor fishermen, and Musa objects before he can stop himself.

quiz.question: What reason is eventually given for damaging the boat?
options: It was old and needed replacing
To protect it from a king who was seizing usable vessels
Khidr disliked the fishermen
It was an accident
quiz.explanation: The boat was damaged to protect it from a king seizing usable vessels.

quiz.question: What does Fajar say is the real instruction of the story?
options: That Musa was a poor prophet
The limits of judging events solely by their visible surface
That miracles should never be questioned
That killing is always justified
quiz.explanation: Fajar says the real instruction is about the limits of judging events solely by their visible surface, not a lesson about specific miracles.

quiz.question: How does Amira describe the effect of the story on the reader?
options: Comforting, since every hardship gets explained
Humbling, since it shows our vantage point is narrower than we assume
Irrelevant to modern life
Frightening without any purpose
quiz.explanation: Amira says the story is humbling rather than comforting, insisting our vantage point is narrower than we assume.

title: Adam's Repentance and the Grammar of Owning a Mistake
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] It's worth noticing what Adam and Hawwa did not say, in that garden, once the fruit of the forbidden tree had already been tasted and the consequence had already begun unfolding.

Narrator: [reflective] There was no elaborate justification offered, no reference to the whisperer who had engineered the moment, no attempt to distribute the fault evenly across every available party.

Narrator: [firm] Their recorded words are almost startling in their economy: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will certainly be among the losers.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Compare that grammar carefully to another well-known refusal in the same narrative, where a different response to failure took an entirely different shape altogether.

Narrator: [reflective] When pride was confronted with its own error, it argued, it compared itself favorably to what it had been asked to honor, it treated the correction as an insult rather than information.

Narrator: [firm] Adam's response contains no such comparison, no appeal to circumstance, no insistence that the fault belonged elsewhere; only a direct admission, addressed upward rather than outward.

Narrator: [warm] What strikes me is how immediately mercy follows that particular grammar, as though the sincerity of the admission itself, more than the severity of the offense, determined what came next.
Narrator: [thoughtful] This doesn't mean consequence vanished entirely; a garden was, after all, exchanged for an earth requiring labor, hardship, and eventual return to dust.

Narrator: [reflective] But exile accompanied by accepted repentance is an entirely different inheritance than exile accompanied by unrepented pride, even when the physical departure looks, from a distance, identical.
Narrator: [warm] I find something quietly instructive in the fact that the very first human error is met not with permanent estrangement but with words offered specifically to be received.
Narrator: [thoughtful] It suggests that repentance was built into the architecture of being human from its earliest chapter, not appended later as a grudging concession to inevitable failure.

Narrator: [peacefully] Every mistake since has had, available to it, that same original grammar: no elaborate defense, simply an honest admission, addressed to the one actually capable of answering it.

quiz.question: What did Adam and Hawwa NOT do after eating from the forbidden tree, according to the narrator?
options: They did not feel any regret
They did not offer elaborate justification or attempt to distribute blame elsewhere
They did not speak to Allah at all
They did not leave the garden
quiz.explanation: They offered no elaborate justification and made no attempt to distribute the fault across other parties.

quiz.question: What was the essential content of Adam and Hawwa's recorded words?
options: A demand for a second chance without admission
An admission that they had wronged themselves, appealing for forgiveness and mercy
A complaint about being tempted unfairly
A request to stay in the garden regardless
quiz.explanation: Their words were: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us we will be among the losers.

quiz.question: How does the narrator contrast this response with the other refusal in the same narrative?
options: Both responses were identical
The other response argued, compared itself favorably, and treated correction as an insult
The other response also admitted fault immediately
There is no other response mentioned
quiz.explanation: The contrasting response argued, compared itself favorably to what it had been asked to honor, and treated correction as an insult rather than information.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say determined what came next after Adam's admission?
options: The severity of the offense alone
The sincerity of the admission itself, more than the severity of the offense
Nothing determined the outcome
A lengthy period of punishment first
quiz.explanation: The narrator suggests the sincerity of the admission, more than the severity of the offense, determined what followed.

quiz.question: What broader idea does the narrator draw about repentance from this story?
options: Repentance was added later as a concession
Repentance was built into the architecture of being human from its earliest chapter
Repentance is only for prophets
Repentance guarantees no consequences at all
quiz.explanation: The narrator concludes repentance was built into the architecture of being human from its earliest chapter, not appended later.

title: Two Visitors, a Scaled Wall, and a Judgment Dawud Nearly Missed
script: Host: [curious] Ustadzah Rina, the story of the two disputants who scaled the wall of Dawud's private chamber is such an odd, almost theatrical way to deliver a lesson. What's actually happening there?

Ustadzah Rina: [pleasant] It is theatrical, deliberately so. Two figures appear where visitors shouldn't be able to reach him, and Dawud, understandably startled, assumes some kind of intrusion or threat.
Host: [interested] But they reassure him quickly, don't they, before presenting what seems like an ordinary property dispute?
Ustadzah Rina: [nodding] Yes, one claims ninety-nine ewes to the other's single ewe, and insists his brother wants to fold that lone ewe into his own already considerable flock.
Host: [thoughtful] A fairly mundane grievance, on the surface, hardly worthy of such an elaborate entrance.
Ustadzah Rina: [firm] And that's precisely what makes Dawud's instant reaction so revealing. He rules immediately, without hearing the second party at all, that the request is indeed unjust.
Host: [surprised] He rules without hearing both sides properly? That seems like a striking lapse for someone renowned for wisdom and judgment.
Ustadzah Rina: [warm] It is, and the text doesn't soften that fact for our comfort. Dawud himself immediately senses he has been tested, and the response is instant, unhesitating repentance.
Host: [curious] What exactly had he been tested on, if the ruling itself was arguably correct on its face?
Ustadzah Rina: [reflective] Not the content of the ruling, but the procedure behind it. Even a familiar-sounding grievance deserves both parties heard, deliberation rather than reflexive certainty.

Ustadzah Rina: [thoughtful] There's also a broader resonance: Dawud himself possessed considerable wealth and wives, and the parable gestures, gently but unmistakably, toward questions of desire and sufficiency.
Host: [thoughtful] So the wall-scaling visitors weren't really about sheep at all.
Ustadzah Rina: [warm] Not primarily, no. They were a mirror, held up abruptly enough that reflexive judgment couldn't dress itself up as careful wisdom before he'd examined it honestly.
Host: [reflective] And his response to being caught in that reflex is itself instructive.
Ustadzah Rina: [gently] Precisely. He fell in prostration and sought forgiveness immediately, without excuse, and that unhesitating humility is arguably the actual point of the whole episode.

quiz.question: How did the two disputants reach Dawud?
options: Through the front gate with an appointment
By scaling the wall of his private chamber
By sending a written letter
Through a public court session
quiz.explanation: Two figures appeared by scaling the wall of Dawud's private chamber, where visitors shouldn't have been able to reach him.

quiz.question: What was the dispute the two men presented?
options: A dispute over land ownership
One claimed ninety-nine ewes while accusing the other, who had one ewe, of wanting it added to his flock
A dispute over a debt
A disagreement about inheritance
quiz.explanation: One claimed ninety-nine ewes and said his brother wanted to fold the other's single ewe into an already large flock.

quiz.question: What mistake did Dawud make in his initial ruling?
options: He ruled in favor of the wrong party entirely
He ruled immediately without hearing the second party at all
He refused to rule on the matter
He asked for a bribe before ruling
quiz.explanation: He ruled immediately that the request was unjust without hearing the second party at all.

quiz.question: According to Ustadzah Rina, what was Dawud actually being tested on?
options: The correctness of the ruling's content
The procedure behind the ruling, since even familiar grievances deserve both parties heard
His wealth and generosity
His physical courage
quiz.explanation: She explains he was tested on the procedure, not the content, since deliberation was needed rather than reflexive certainty.

quiz.question: How did Dawud respond once he realized he had been tested?
options: He denied any wrongdoing
He fell in prostration and sought forgiveness immediately, without excuse
He questioned the two visitors further
He punished the visitors for intruding
quiz.explanation: He fell in prostration and sought forgiveness immediately, without excuse, which is presented as the point of the episode.

title: Ibrahim's Argument With an Empire That Worshipped Itself
script: Narrator: [measured] Long before the fire, before the catapult and the miraculous coolness that followed it, Ibrahim's rebellion against his community began with something far quieter: a question asked, apparently, in genuine curiosity.
Narrator: [reflective] He asked his father why he devoted himself to carved objects that could neither hear a request nor answer one, a question so simple it barely qualifies as confrontation.

Narrator: [thoughtful] Rebuffed, he escalated methodically rather than dramatically, reasoning through celestial bodies one by one, testing each candidate for worship against a single, ruthless criterion: does it endure?
Narrator: [firm] A star, admired at dusk, disappeared by dawn, disqualifying itself simply by vanishing. The moon followed the same pattern, luminous and then, predictably, gone.
Narrator: [reflective] Even the sun, grander than either, submitted to the identical logic; magnificence that sets is magnificence still ultimately governed by something greater than itself.

Narrator: [thoughtful] Only then did he arrive at his actual conclusion, that his devotion belonged to whoever had originated the heavens and earth entirely, a reasoning built from observation rather than merely inherited assumption.
Narrator: [wry] The idols themselves he later dismantled physically, smashing every one except the largest, upon whose shoulder he hung the axe, inviting his community to interrogate the survivor.

Narrator: [dry] Brought before the assembly, he suggested, with an almost audible straight face, that they simply ask the largest idol what had happened, since it was, after all, standing right there.
Narrator: [firm] The crowd's own logic collapsed under the question; they knew perfectly well stone doesn't speak, and yet condemning him required momentarily pretending it might.
Narrator: [somber] Unable to answer the argument, the empire answered instead with fire, constructing a blaze large enough that ordinary methods of ignition proved insufficient for the task.

Narrator: [warm] The famous instruction that followed, that the fire be coolness and safety for him, doesn't erase the flames; it simply reminds us that the one who kindles need not be the one who governs.

Narrator: [peacefully] What endures from that episode isn't chiefly the miracle, remarkable as it is, but the method preceding it: patient, escalating reasoning, offered to people who preferred inherited certainty to any actual scrutiny.

quiz.question: How did Ibrahim's rebellion against his community begin, according to the narrator?
options: With an act of violence against the idols
With a quiet question asked in apparent genuine curiosity
With a public speech to the whole town
With a direct confrontation with the king
quiz.explanation: It began with a quiet question to his father about why he worshipped carved objects that could neither hear nor answer.

quiz.question: What criterion did Ibrahim use to test the star, moon, and sun as objects of worship?
options: Their brightness
Whether they endured, since each one eventually set or disappeared
Their size
Their color
quiz.explanation: He tested each against whether it endured; the star, moon, and sun all disqualified themselves by setting or disappearing.

quiz.question: What did Ibrahim do to the idols, leaving one exception?
options: He hid them all
He smashed every one except the largest, hanging the axe on its shoulder
He painted over them
He sold them
quiz.explanation: He smashed every idol except the largest, upon whose shoulder he hung the axe.

quiz.question: What suggestion did Ibrahim make to the assembled crowd?
options: That they rebuild the idols immediately
That they simply ask the largest idol what had happened, since it was standing right there
That they punish him without question
That they abandon idol worship immediately
quiz.explanation: He suggested they ask the largest idol what happened, since it was right there, exposing the absurdity of their belief.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say endures most from this episode?
options: Only the miracle of the fire becoming cool
The method of patient, escalating reasoning offered to people who preferred inherited certainty
The destruction of the idols alone
The size of the fire built against him
quiz.explanation: The narrator says what endures is chiefly the method of patient, escalating reasoning, not merely the miracle of the fire.

title: The Conquest That Chose Not to Look Like One
script: Host: [curious] Pak Darmawan, when people imagine a conquering army entering a city that had exiled and warred against its leader for years, they imagine reprisal. Mecca offers something quite different.
Pak Darmawan: [thoughtful] It does, and that difference is precisely why the episode rewards close attention rather than a quick, congratulatory summary.
Host: [interested] Remind our listeners of the history briefly. These weren't strangers to Muhammad; this was the city that had boycotted, tortured, and driven out his followers.
Pak Darmawan: [measured] Exactly, and some of the very people now facing him at the gates of their own defeated city had orchestrated or celebrated those earlier cruelties directly.
Host: [pointed] So there was ample precedent, even by the standards of the era, for a punitive entrance.
Pak Darmawan: [nodding] Ample precedent, and considerable expectation of it, too. Many in Mecca braced for exactly that outcome, having calculated the odds and prepared accordingly for the worst.
Host: [curious] What happened instead?
Pak Darmawan: [warm] He entered, by most accounts, in a posture of humility rather than triumph, and when the city was fully secured, he asked the assembled Meccans what they expected of him.
Host: [interested] And their answer?
Pak Darmawan: [reflective] They answered, tellingly, that they expected good, invoking the memory of him as a noble brother and a noble nephew, appealing to a relationship rather than a right.
Host: [thoughtful] What was his reply?

Pak Darmawan: [firm] Go, for you are free, echoing almost precisely the words Yusuf once offered his own brothers centuries earlier, a deliberate, unmistakable allusion for anyone who knew the older story.
Host: [reflective] That's a striking parallel, forgiveness at the height of power, extended to people who had shown him none.
Pak Darmawan: [thoughtful] It is, and I think the parallel is intentional rather than coincidental, given how thoroughly that earlier story would have been known to everyone listening that day.
Host: [warm] What does that restraint actually communicate, in your view, beyond simple mercy?
Pak Darmawan: [warm] That power exercised without cruelty isn't weakness pretending otherwise; it's often the clearest demonstration available of what real strength was for in the first place.

quiz.question: What history did Mecca have with Muhammad before the conquest, according to the discussion?
options: A peaceful, uneventful relationship
The city had boycotted, tortured, and driven out his followers
They had always been allies
There was no prior conflict
quiz.explanation: Mecca was the city that had boycotted, tortured, and driven out his followers, with some now facing him at the gates.

quiz.question: What did many in Mecca expect when the city was defeated?
options: A peaceful welcome
A punitive entrance, given ample historical precedent
Immediate exile of all citizens
No consequences at all
quiz.explanation: Many in Mecca braced for a punitive entrance, having calculated the odds and prepared for the worst.

quiz.question: How did Muhammad enter the city, according to Pak Darmawan?
options: In a posture of triumph and celebration
In a posture of humility rather than triumph
Accompanied by a punitive display of force
Secretly, avoiding public attention
quiz.explanation: By most accounts, he entered in a posture of humility rather than triumph.

quiz.question: What answer did the Meccans give when asked what they expected of him?
options: They expected punishment
They expected good, invoking his memory as a noble brother and nephew
They refused to answer
They demanded he leave the city
quiz.explanation: They answered that they expected good, invoking the memory of him as a noble brother and a noble nephew.

quiz.question: What earlier story does Muhammad's reply, 'Go, for you are free,' deliberately echo?
options: The story of Musa and Pharaoh
Yusuf's words to the brothers who had wronged him
The story of Nuh's flood
There is no intended echo
quiz.explanation: The reply echoes almost precisely the words Yusuf once offered his own brothers, a deliberate allusion.

title: Sulaiman, the Ant, and an Army That Learned to Listen
script: Narrator: [reflective] Sulaiman's story is often remembered for its scale, kingdoms, jinn, winds commanded at will, and it's easy, amid all that grandeur, to overlook the moment involving a single, unremarkable ant.

Narrator: [thoughtful] Marching his considerable army through a valley, he heard, or was made to understand, an ant instructing its colony to retreat quickly, lest Sulaiman's forces crush them without ever noticing.

Narrator: [warm] What happened next is the detail worth sitting with: he smiled, genuinely amused and moved, and immediately halted an army of extraordinary scale for the sake of insects he'd never otherwise have registered.

Narrator: [reflective] Power of that magnitude rarely pauses for anything so small; empires are built, historically, on the assumption that smallness simply doesn't register on the ledger of consequence.

Narrator: [firm] Yet Sulaiman's response wasn't merely tolerance; it was gratitude, praying explicitly to be kept thankful for blessings that included, apparently, the very capacity to overhear an ant's warning at all.

Narrator: [thoughtful] That gratitude is instructive precisely because it wasn't directed at the grand blessings alone, the throne, the command of wind and jinn, but at something almost comically minor by comparison.

Narrator: [reflective] Elsewhere in his story, a similarly humbling posture recurs: the hoopoe bird's report of a queen ruling a prosperous kingdom that worshipped the sun rather than its actual originator.

Narrator: [thoughtful] Sulaiman didn't dismiss information arriving from something so unlikely as a bird; he verified it carefully, then acted through invitation and diplomacy rather than immediate, overwhelming force.
Narrator: [warm] The letter he sent the queen was notably restrained in tone, an invitation to consider truth rather than a demand issued from unquestionable strength.

Narrator: [reflective] She, for her part, responded with unusual political shrewdness, testing his intentions with gifts before ultimately visiting him and recognizing, on her own reasoning, where true sovereignty actually resided.
Narrator: [thoughtful] What connects the ant and the queen, oddly enough, is the same quality: a ruler secure enough in real power to listen carefully to voices far beneath his evident station.
Narrator: [peacefully] Sulaiman's kingdom is remembered for its vastness, certainly, but perhaps it should be remembered equally for how attentively that vastness bent down to notice what was small.

quiz.question: What did the ant instruct its colony to do as Sulaiman's army approached?
options: To attack the army
To retreat quickly so they would not be crushed unnoticed
To hide underground permanently
To ignore the army completely
quiz.explanation: The ant instructed its colony to retreat quickly, lest Sulaiman's forces crush them without ever noticing.

quiz.question: How did Sulaiman respond upon hearing the ant's warning?
options: He ignored it and continued marching
He smiled, was genuinely moved, and halted his army for the sake of the ants
He punished the ant for speaking
He ordered the valley destroyed
quiz.explanation: He smiled, genuinely amused and moved, and immediately halted his extraordinary army for the ants' sake.

quiz.question: What did Sulaiman pray for after this encounter?
options: A larger kingdom
To be kept thankful for his blessings, including the capacity to overhear the ant's warning
Victory over all his enemies
Longer life
quiz.explanation: He prayed explicitly to be kept thankful for blessings that included the capacity to overhear an ant's warning at all.

quiz.question: What information did the hoopoe bird bring to Sulaiman?
options: News of an approaching storm
A report of a queen ruling a prosperous kingdom that worshipped the sun
News of a hidden treasure
A request for help from another kingdom
quiz.explanation: The hoopoe reported a queen ruling a prosperous kingdom that worshipped the sun rather than its actual originator.

quiz.question: What quality does the narrator say connects the ant episode and the queen episode?
options: Sulaiman's wealth
A ruler secure enough in real power to listen carefully to voices far beneath his station
Sulaiman's military strength
The size of his kingdom alone
quiz.explanation: The narrator says both episodes show a ruler secure enough in real power to listen carefully to voices far beneath his evident station.
